78.title: The child at the well
78.hook: Mencius: anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that is the seed of goodness (Mencius 2A.6)
78.howItsDone: Students of Confucian thought learn the child at the well as Mencius's case that human nature is good; it has been memorized and debated in East Asian schools for many centuries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Good Samaritan stopped on the Jericho road. Your line was go and do likewise. Who did you stop for? Day seventy-eight.

A new week, and a week of many houses: China, India, the Sikh Gurus, the Gospels and the Buddha, one story from each, each kept by its own people. We begin with a question you've probably argued about at some point. Are people basically good? Or basically selfish, and just good at hiding it? The news on a bad day will give you one answer. A stranger carrying your groceries will give you the other. About twenty-three centuries ago, a Chinese philosopher named Mencius answered with a picture that takes about two seconds to imagine. Today's story is the child at the well.
screen: `A WEEK OF MANY HOUSES.` → `ARE PEOPLE BASICALLY GOOD?` → `A TWO-SECOND PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Mencius lived in the three hundreds BCE. He was a teacher in the line of Confucius, and the tradition came to call him the second sage, honored next to Confucius himself. The book of his teachings is simply called the Mencius. In one passage, he says every person has a heart that can't bear to see others suffer. And here's his proof. Suppose someone suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and distress. And then he rules out the other explanations one by one. It isn't because you want to get in good with the child's parents. It isn't because you want your neighbors and friends to praise you. It isn't because you'd dislike what people would say, or, as some read the line, the sound of the child crying. It's there before any of that. It's just there. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say everyone runs and saves the child. The picture stops at the jolt, the first flash, before any decision. That flash, Mencius says, is a sprout. He names four of them: the heart of compassion, the heart of shame, the heart of courtesy, and the heart that knows right from wrong. Everyone has them, like having four limbs. But sprouts have to be grown, like a small fire catching or a spring starting to flow. Not every Confucian agreed. A later thinker named Xunzi argued the opposite: that goodness has to be trained into people from the outside. Chinese tradition kept both voices. But Mencius's picture is hard to shake. The next time you flinch at someone else's pain, that's it. That's the seed.
screen: `MENCIUS, IN THE LINE OF CONFUCIUS.` · `A CHILD ABOUT TO FALL.` · `NOT FOR PRAISE, NOT FOR THANKS.` · `FOUR SPROUTS, TO BE GROWN.` · then, large: `THE SEED IS THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your first kind impulse today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Was there a moment when something in you leaned toward someone else: a wince when a friend was hurt, a wish to help a stranger, a flash of care before you thought about it? Find one. Don't judge whether you acted on it. Just notice that it was there, before any reasons arrived. That's one of Mencius's sprouts. Let your attention rest on it, like sun on a seedling. The bell holds the time.
The child at the well. Mencius's picture of the jolt anyone feels, before any reason, and the sprout of goodness inside it. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHILD AT THE WELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the seed is there. Today, when you feel that first small pull toward someone, notice it, and give it a little water. Day seventy-eight.

79.title: The river passes
79.hook: Confucius stands by a river and says it flows on like this, day and night (Analects 9.16)
79.howItsDone: The line from the Analects is one of the best known in Chinese, often quoted when people speak of passing time, and Confucian scholars have long read it as both a lament and a call to steady effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mencius and the child at the well, and the jolt of care that comes before any reason. Your line was the seed is there. Did you catch a sprout? Day seventy-nine.

Have you ever stood on a bridge and just watched the water go under? It's oddly hard to walk away from. The water you're looking at is gone before you've finished looking, and yet the river stays exactly where it is. Kids stare at it. Old people stare at it. Nobody has to explain why. Two and a half thousand years ago in China, a teacher stood on a riverbank with his students, looked at the water for a while, and said one short sentence. People have been arguing about what he meant ever since. Today's story is the river passes.
screen: `WATCHING WATER FROM A BRIDGE.` → `GONE, AND STILL THERE.` → `ONE SENTENCE BY A RIVER.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Confucius, and the sentence is in the Analects, the collection of his sayings gathered by his students after his death. In James Legge's old translation, it reads: "The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'" That's the whole passage. No explanation. No moral. Just a man watching water and saying: like this. And because he didn't explain, readers have heard two very different things in it. Some hear a sigh. Time is running away, like water, day and night, and we're getting older on the bank. Confucius was an old man by the end, and he'd spent his life hoping a ruler would put his teaching to use, and none really did. Heard that way, it's gentle grief about time. Others hear encouragement. The river doesn't stop. It doesn't rest on its good days or quit on its bad ones. It just keeps going, and over years it cuts through rock. Mencius, whom we met yesterday, praised water that comes from a real spring, because it flows on day and night and fills every hollow before moving on. Later Confucian scholars heard in the river the ceaseless working of the world itself. You don't have to choose. Maybe both are true at once. Time does pass. And the way to meet passing time is to keep flowing with it, a little each day. In Greece, around the same era, Heraclitus said you can't step into the same river twice. Two thinkers who never met, both watching water.
screen: `CONFUCIUS AT THE STREAM.` · `A SIGH ABOUT PASSING TIME.` · `OR: KEEP FLOWING, LIKE WATER.` · `MAYBE BOTH AT ONCE.` · then, large: `DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch water move, for the length of the sit. If you're near a river, a fountain, rain, or even a tap you can run slowly, watch it. If not, pour a glass and watch the surface settle, or picture a stream you've known. Settle, and breathe. Watch the water arrive and leave. Don't try to hold any of it. Notice your own breath doing the same thing, in and out, never the same breath twice. Just like this. The bell holds the time.
The river passes. Confucius's one sentence at the stream: it goes on like this, day and night. A sigh, or a push, or both. Today's word.
Your line: day and night. Today, pick one small thing you want to keep doing, and do a little of it, the way a river keeps going. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: Satyakama tells the truth
80.hook: asked his family line, the boy tells the plain truth about his mother, and the teacher accepts him for it (Chandogya Upanishad 4.4)
80.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and readers of the Upanishads often tell the story of Satyakama Jabala as a lesson in truthfulness, and it is widely discussed in debates about birth, caste and fitness to learn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the river passes: Confucius at the stream, and water that keeps going. Your line was day and night. What did you keep flowing? Day eighty.

Think of a form that asks a question you'd rather not answer. Father's name. Previous address. Reason for leaving your last job. There's always a small temptation to round the answer off, to make it sound tidier than your life actually was. Almost everyone has felt that. Now imagine the question is asked out loud, by a teacher you desperately want to study with, and the honest answer is: I don't know who my father is. That's where a boy named Satyakama found himself, in one of the oldest books in India. Today's story is Satyakama tells the truth.
screen: `A FORM YOU'D RATHER NOT FILL.` → `THE TIDY ANSWER.` → `THE HONEST ONE.`

segments.voice: It's in the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the oldest Upanishads, the philosophical texts that close the Vedas, probably composed well before the Buddha's time. A boy named Satyakama wants to become a student of the sacred teaching. In that world, a teacher would ask a new student his family line, his gotra. So Satyakama asks his mother, Jabala: what is my family line? And she tells him the truth. When I was young, she says, I moved around a great deal, working as a servant, and that's when I had you. I don't know your family line. My name is Jabala. Your name is Satyakama. Call yourself Satyakama Jabala. That's it. No cover story. So the boy goes to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama. The teacher asks: what is your family line? And Satyakama repeats his mother's words, exactly, in front of everyone. And the teacher says, as the Upanishad tells it, that only a true Brahmin could speak like that. Go and fetch firewood, he says: I'll take you as my student, because you have not turned away from the truth. His name, by the way, means something like one who loves truth: satya, truth, and kama, desire. Scholars read the teacher's answer in different ways. Some hear a radical idea, that truthfulness, not birth, is what makes a person fit to learn. Others point out that the story still speaks inside the world of caste, and simply finds its highest mark in a boy's honesty. Either way, look at who the heroes are: a mother who didn't lie to her son, and a son who didn't lie for her.
screen: `WHAT IS MY FAMILY LINE?` · `JABALA'S HONEST ANSWER.` · `HE REPEATS IT, WORD FOR WORD.` · `YOU HAVE NOT TURNED FROM TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one plain truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place in your life where you usually round things off. Maybe it's I'm fine, when you're not. Maybe it's a small exaggeration, or a detail you always leave out. You don't have to confess anything big. Just picture saying the plain version, once, kindly, to someone safe. Notice the fear that comes, and notice that you're still here. Satyakama's knees probably shook too. The bell holds the time.
Satyakama tells the truth. The boy with no family line to give, who gave the truth instead, and was taken as a student for it. Today's word.
Your line: the truth is enough. Today, when you feel the pull to tidy up an answer, say the plain version instead, kindly. Day eighty.

81.title: Honest bread
81.hook: Guru Nanak squeezes a poor carpenter's bread and it drips milk, a rich man's bread and it drips blood (Janamsakhi tradition)
81.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, honest work, alongside sharing and remembering God; the langar, the free kitchen at every gurdwara, shares food with anyone who comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyakama tells the truth: no family line to give, so he gave the truth, and was taken in. Your line was the truth is enough. What plain truth did you tell? Day eighty-one.

Two invitations to dinner arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town: a big feast, the best food, everyone important will be there. The other is from a carpenter who lives down a side street, and dinner is a plain, rough flatbread made from a cheap grain. You know which one most people would pick. And you probably know which one the guest of honor in today's story picked. The guest is Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, and the story is about what's inside a loaf of bread. Today's story is honest bread.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `THE RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `THE CARPENTER'S ROUGH BREAD.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak lived from 1469 to 1539, in Punjab, and Sikhs honor him as the founder of their path. Many stories about his life are kept in collections called the Janamsakhis, written down by his followers in the generations after him. Sikhs treasure them as stories of the Guru, and they're separate from the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the story. On his travels, Guru Nanak comes to the town of Saidpur and stays with a poor carpenter named Bhai Lalo, eating the simple bread Lalo earns with his own hands. A wealthy official named Malik Bhago is holding a great feast, and he's offended that the famous holy man is staying in a carpenter's hut. He demands that Nanak come. When Nanak arrives, Bhago asks why he refused his fine food. So Nanak asks for two pieces of bread: one from Bhago's feast, and one from Lalo's kitchen. He holds one in each hand and squeezes. From Lalo's bread, the story says, drips milk. From Bhago's, drips blood. Bread made by honest work, and bread made by squeezing the poor. Whatever you make of the miracle, the point is plain. For Sikhs it's one of the three pillars of life: kirat karni, earning an honest living; vand chhakna, sharing what you have; and naam japna, remembering God. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib says it simply: the one who earns by their own work and gives some away has found the path. And Lalo? His name even appears in one of Guru Nanak's hymns in the scripture. The carpenter got remembered. The feast didn't.
screen: `GURU NANAK AND THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `LALO'S HUT, BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.` · `EARN HONESTLY, SHARE, REMEMBER.` · then, large: `HONEST BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something honestly made. If you have something to eat nearby, a piece of bread, some fruit, a cup of tea, hold it. If not, think of your last meal. Settle, and breathe. Think of the hands it passed through: someone planted it, picked it, carried it, baked it, stocked the shelf. Then think of your own hands, and the work that paid for it. Take a slow bite or sip if you can, and taste it properly. Let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
Honest bread. The carpenter's rough bread that, in the story, dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand, because it was earned without harming anyone. Today's word.
Your line: honest bread. Today, at one meal, think of the hands that made it, and share one small piece of what you have. Day eighty-one.

82.title: Feet toward the Kaaba
82.hook: resting at Mecca, Nanak is told to move his feet away from God's house, and asks where God is not (Janamsakhi tradition)
82.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Mecca story from the Janamsakhis to teach that God is present everywhere; Muslims face the Kaaba in prayer as the direction that unites them, while teaching that God is not confined to any place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, honest bread: Lalo's rough loaf that dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand. Your line was honest bread. Whose hands did you think of at your meal? Day eighty-two.

Most of us have a place where we lower our voices without being told. A church, a mosque, a temple, a grandmother's living room, a grave. Something in the body knows to be careful there. And most of us have seen someone get it wrong: shoes on where they should be off, a laugh at the wrong moment, feet up on the wrong chair. Today's story, from the Sikh tradition, starts with exactly that kind of moment: a tired traveler at the holiest place in Islam, lying down with his feet pointing the wrong way. Today's story is feet toward the Kaaba.
screen: `A PLACE WHERE WE GO QUIET.` → `FEET ON THE WRONG CHAIR.` → `A TRAVELER AT MECCA.`

segments.voice: The Janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak we met yesterday, say that on one of his long journeys he traveled west, as far as Mecca. Muslim histories don't record this visit, and historians debate whether it happened as told. But Sikhs have loved the story for centuries. Here's how it goes. Nanak arrives tired and lies down to sleep near the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the center of the Grand Mosque, which Muslims around the world face when they pray. His feet are pointing toward it. A local religious official finds him, and he's upset, and you can understand why. To him it looks like deep disrespect. He tells Nanak to take his feet away from the house of God. And Nanak answers, as the story is told: then please turn my feet in a direction where God is not. In some versions, the official grabs his feet and drags them around, and wherever the feet point, the Kaaba seems to be there. In others, the words alone are enough. Either way, the official goes quiet. Here's what makes the story generous rather than a put-down. Muslims teach this too. The Kaaba is the direction of prayer, the house dedicated to God, not a place God is kept. The Qur'an says that to God belong the east and the west, and wherever you turn, there is the face of God. So the official and the Guru aren't really on opposite sides. Nanak just asked the question out loud. And it's a question you can carry anywhere. If there's something sacred, where is it not? The kitchen floor. The bus. The ground under your feet right now.
screen: `NANAK REACHES MECCA.` · `HIS FEET POINT AT THE KAABA.` · `TURN THEM WHERE GOD IS NOT.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, THE FACE OF GOD.` · then, large: `WHERE IS IT NOT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel the ground under your feet. Sit with both feet flat on the floor, or stand if you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Notice the soles of your feet: the pressure, the temperature, the floor pushing back. Whatever this ground is, carpet, concrete, grass, it's holding you up without being asked. Let your attention rest there. If you have a sense of the sacred, let yourself ask Nanak's question quietly: is it here too? If you don't, simply notice being held. The bell holds the time.
Feet toward the Kaaba. Guru Nanak's answer when told to move his feet from God's house: then turn them where God is not. Today's word.
Your line: where is it not. Today, in one ordinary place, a kitchen, a parking lot, a hallway, pause for one breath and ask it. Day eighty-two.

83.title: The prodigal son
83.hook: a father runs down the road to a son who wasted everything (Luke 15:11–32)
83.howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the prodigal son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns, and it is read often in churches, especially in seasons of repentance such as Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, feet toward the Kaaba, and Guru Nanak's question. Your line was where is it not. Where did you pause and ask it? Day eighty-three.

Think of the text you've been putting off. The one to someone you let down, or drifted from, or said something to that you regret. Maybe you've drafted it in your head a dozen times. Hey, I know it's been a while. I know I messed up. You rehearse the apology until it's perfect, and you picture every way it could go wrong. Jesus told a story about a young man doing exactly that, rehearsing his apology the whole long walk home. And the story's great surprise is what happens before he gets to say it. Today's story is the prodigal son.
screen: `THE TEXT YOU'VE BEEN PUTTING OFF.` → `THE REHEARSED APOLOGY.` → `A LONG WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: It's in Luke, chapter fifteen, the third in a row of stories about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. A man has two sons. The younger one asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is still alive, which in that world was close to saying: I wish you were dead. The father gives it. The son goes to a far country and spends it all. Then a famine comes, and he ends up feeding pigs, so hungry he'd have eaten their food. And then, in the King James words, "when he came to himself." He decides to go home and say: I've sinned; I'm not worthy to be your son; take me on as a hired worker. He rehearses it. And here's the verse the whole story turns on: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father saw him from far off, so he'd been watching the road. And he ran. Grown men of standing didn't usually run in public; commentators love this detail. The son starts his speech, and the father doesn't even let him finish. Bring the best robe, a ring, shoes; kill the fattened calf. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But there's a second son, out in the field, furious that the waster gets a party. And the father goes out to him too. The story ends without telling us whether the older brother comes in. Christians read the father as a picture of God's welcome. The door is open for both sons. The ending is left to us.
screen: `THREE LOST THINGS.` · `THE SON WASTES IT ALL.` · `WHEN HE CAME TO HIMSELF.` · `THE FATHER SAW HIM, AND RAN.` · then, large: `HE RAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone back. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who's drifted from you, or who let you down, or who you've been waiting to hear from. Picture them far off down a road. You don't have to decide anything today. Just notice what your heart does as you see them there. Does it tighten, or lean forward? Now picture taking one step toward them, before any apology is finished. Just one. If the one who drifted is you, picture the father seeing you. The bell holds the time.
The prodigal son. The son who wasted everything and came home, and the father who saw him a long way off, and ran. Today's word.
Your line: he ran. Today, if someone reaches back toward you, meet them before their apology is done. Or send the first short message yourself. Day eighty-three.

84.title: The raft
84.hook: the Buddha: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (Majjhima Nikaya 22)
84.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the simile of the raft to explain that the teachings are tools for liberation rather than possessions to cling to or argue over.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prodigal son, and a father who saw him far off. Your line was he ran. Did you take a step toward someone? Day eighty-four.

Look back at this week of many houses. Mencius and the child at the well. Confucius watching the river. Satyakama's plain truth. Guru Nanak's honest bread, and his feet toward the Kaaba. A father running down a road. Chinese, Hindu, Sikh and Christian stories, each from its own home. We end the week with the Buddha, and a story about something every one of those traditions has: methods. Ways of praying, sitting, learning. Useful things. And the odd question of what to do with a useful thing once it's done its job. Today's story is the raft.
screen: `A WEEK OF MANY HOUSES.` → `EVERY PATH HAS METHODS.` → `WHEN A METHOD HAS DONE ITS JOB.`

segments.voice: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, number twenty-two. The Buddha tells his monks: imagine a man on a long journey who comes to a wide river. The near bank is dangerous and frightening. The far bank is safe. There's no ferry and no bridge. So he gathers grass and sticks and branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddling with his hands and feet, he makes it across. Now he's on the safe side, and he thinks: this raft was so useful to me. I should pick it up and carry it on my head wherever I go. And the Buddha asks the monks: would that man be doing the right thing with the raft? No, they say. What he should do, the Buddha says, is pull it up on the shore, or leave it floating, and go on his way. And then he says the startling part: in the same way, the teaching itself is like a raft. It's for crossing over, not for holding onto. Think about who's saying that. The Buddha is talking about his own teaching. Buddhists have discussed for centuries exactly what letting go of it means. It doesn't mean the teaching is useless; he just spent the whole story saying how useful the raft was. It means don't cling to it, don't turn it into something to own and defend. Use it to cross. You know this from ordinary life. The training wheels. The flashcards. The alarm you needed for years and then didn't. There's no shame in how much you needed a raft. The only mistake is carrying it on your head after you've reached the shore.
screen: `A WIDE RIVER, NO BRIDGE.` · `GRASS, STICKS, HANDS AND FEET.` · `CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD?` · `THE TEACHING IS FOR CROSSING.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE RAFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put down one method that's done its job. Settle, and breathe. Think about the habits, rules and tricks you use to get through a day. Is there one you're still carrying out of habit, after it stopped helping? A way of working that fit an old job. A rule you made in a hard season that's over now. Find one. Thank it, honestly; it got you across something. Now picture setting it down on the bank, gently, and walking on a few steps without it. The bell holds the time.
The raft. The Buddha's picture of a teaching as something for crossing over, useful, and then set down on the far shore. Today's word.
Your line: leave the raft. Today, notice one thing you do only because you've always done it, and ask whether you've already crossed. Day eighty-four.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: the Buddha says the raft was useless
it carried the man across. the point is not to cling to it afterward.
the Buddha applies the raft to his own teaching
the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding onto.
the man should carry the raft on his head
he should pull it ashore or leave it floating, and go on.

fork.setup: you've crossed the river on a raft you built. you're safe on the far bank. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head, in gratitude
leave it on the shore and go on
burn it so no one else can use it
fork.reveal: leave it: pull it ashore or let it float, and go on. the Buddha says his own teaching is like that raft, for crossing, not for holding.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: kulla, a raft. the simile of the raft is the kullupama.

trapdoor: what you thought: once you're done with something, throw it away.
what it means: use the teaching to cross, and don't cling to it or carry it as a burden.
what a scholar hears: the raft simile sits in MN 22, the Alagaddupama Sutta, beside the simile of the water snake.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)
